cards.headline: Canada reimposes sanctions against 11 Iranian companies

pages.text: Canada is reimposing sanctions against 11 Iranian companies in the energy and banking sectors to disrupt financial networks that support Iran's nuclear program, according to a statement from the Canadian foreign ministry. The ministry issued the statement on the sidelines of a G7 meeting in Paris, alleging the companies contribute to Iran's nuclear drive, ballistic missile program, or the financing of “malign activities.” The sanctioned entities include the National Iranian Oil Company and the banks Mellat and Melli. These companies were previously delisted from Canadian sanctions in 2016.

cards.headline: At least 17 people killed in Turkey steel factory explosion

pages.text: An explosion and subsequent fire at the Habas Demir Celik iron and steel plant in Aliaga, near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey, has killed at least 17 people and injured 12 others. The incident occurred at approximately 11:46am local time on November 9, 2026, during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces. All those killed and injured were workers at the facility, which is one of the country's leading steel producers. Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban stated that some people were believed to still be under the rubble as search and rescue operations continued. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and noted that investigations are underway. While the President originally stated the death toll was 16, Health Minister Kemal Memişoğlu later announced that one person who had been critically injured had died, bringing the total to at least 17.

The explosion was triggered when a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below. One worker told AFP that a snapped crane cable sent approximately 120 tonnes of molten steel crashing onto the furnace, triggering a violent reaction. Governor Elban added that the collapse damaged a gas line, causing the blast. Eyewitnesses reported that the explosion shook the ground, with some initially believing an earthquake had occurred. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air. At the time of the accident, fewer than the usual number of employees were in the affected area because production had been suspended for maintenance; approximately 200 employees were present. Following the disaster, local media reports cited by BBC News's Turkish service stated that at least five people have been arrested. Four prosecutors have been assigned to investigate the circumstances of the event.

cards.headline: Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles fired toward Riyadh and southern region

pages.text: Saudi Arabian forces intercepted two missiles fired toward the capital, Riyadh, and a third missile aimed at the country's southern region. The Saudi-led coalition, which is fighting Yemen’s Houthis, reported that a ballistic missile and a cruise missile were destroyed over Riyadh, while a second ballistic missile was downed over the southern part of the country, according to Major-General Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the coalition. Al-Maliki blamed the Iran-backed Houthis for the attacks. In Riyadh, residents received text-message alerts to take shelter due to an “aerial threat,” and the AFP news agency reported multiple explosions. The country’s civil defence agency later issued a message stating the danger had passed. These missile strikes occurred hours after reports of damage to a key East-West pipeline.

The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported that Saudi-led coalition air strikes hit Sanaa, the Yemeni capital controlled by the Houthis. According to Saba, the strikes hit a building belonging to the state oil company in southern Sanaa and the al-Mufazir gas facility in the Jadar district, north of the capital. Civil defence teams were reportedly working to extinguish a fire in gas trailers at the al-Mufazir station. The coalition did not immediately confirm these strikes. Meanwhile, Yemen’s armed forces, representing the internationally recognised government, stated they carried out 874 attacks on Houthi targets during the past several hours as part of the “Dawn of Yemen” operation. Military spokesperson Majed Al-Nuzaili said these air and ground strikes killed or wounded approximately 190 Houthi commanders and fighters. Al-Nuzaili also reported that initial field estimates indicated the strikes destroyed or damaged about 130 Houthi military vehicles and equipment, as well as positions and fortifications.

cards.headline: US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as trilateral talks begin in Abu Dhabi

pages.text: US officials have stated they are seeking a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine through trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi. These represent the first substantive peace talks between the two countries since February. A central component of the Trump administration’s proposal involves creating a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe. A US administration official noted that the US would “need Europe at the table” to reach an end to the conflict. The first day of talks concluded in the early afternoon local time, with a second day scheduled to follow.

European officials expressed concern that Russia may maintain demands for NATO to reduce its military footprint across eastern Europe. Such a rollback could leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence during a period of historic tensions with the West. Before the trilateral talks, European officials held separate discussions with representatives from the US and Ukraine. In a joint statement, they agreed that any future arrangements must respect the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independent decision-making of Ukraine, while providing credible security guarantees for the country. European leaders remain skeptical of Russia's intentions; EU high representative for foreign policy Kaja Kallas told Reuters on November 9, 2026, that Russia has appeared to be “pretending that they negotiate” because no goodwill has been observed from the Russian side.

The negotiations occur amid internal and regional pressures. The talks follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home and follow US-led joint strikes with Israel against Iran. Additionally, European leaders have expressed unease regarding the variety of peace talk strands. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the process of meetings and phone calls as “disorderly,” arguing it weakens Europe’s ability to speak with one voice. While Vladimir Putin has sought to renegotiate the balance of power between NATO and Russia by complaining about NATO's eastward expansion for over a decade, a sitting US administration has not previously embraced those demands.

cards.headline: Malaysian court clears former PM Najib Razak for house arrest transfer

pages.text: A Kuala Lumpur High Court has cleared the way for jailed former Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak to be transferred to house arrest following a dispute over his legal status. Kuala Lumpur High Court Judge Aslam Zainuddin stated that, in accordance with the order of a conditional pardon, Najib shall serve the remainder of a reduced six-year prison sentence under house arrest. This order applies only to Najib's first conviction. Najib, 73, was previously jailed for his role in the theft of public funds from the now-defunct 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB), described as one of the largest global plunders of a sovereign wealth fund. On November 6, 2026, Najib’s political party paid a $12 million fine as part of the terms of a royal pardon, and he was scheduled to leave prison at that time.

The transfer to house arrest was previously postponed after the attorney general intervened, raising questions regarding the legal interpretation of the royal pardon and the court order allowing Najib to leave jail. The intervention caused political and constitutional controversy in Malaysia. King Sultan Ibrahim warned that any attempt to challenge his order to allow Najib to leave jail and move to house arrest could amount to defiance against his decree. In Malaysia, the king holds a position rotated among nine regional sultans; while the role is largely ceremonial, the king has the authority to grant pardons under discretionary powers granted by the Malaysian Constitution.

cards.headline: Global carbon pollution dropped 0.4% in 2026 due to energy shocks from the war in Iran

pages.text: Global carbon dioxide emissions from burning fossil fuels, such as coal, oil, and gas, fell by 0.4% in 2026 to 42.2 billion tons (38.2 billion metric tons). Scientists from the Global Carbon Project say this slight decrease was largely driven by energy shocks resulting from the war in Iran rather than progress in fighting climate change. This marks the third time in the 21st century that global carbon pollution has dropped. According to study co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway, the decline is primarily due to the war in Iran and its impact on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping artery for petroleum products. Peters stated that the war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, which pushed up global prices for gasoline and oil. He noted that the timing and the specific types of fuel emission drops make the team certain the decline was related to these war-triggered energy shocks.

The Global Carbon Project, which publishes its estimates in the journal Earth System Science Data Discussions, utilized an international team of more than 140 scientists to calculate these yearly emissions figures. The team used data from around the world, including estimates for the final months of the year, to reach their findings. The study found that oil emissions dropped nearly 2% and natural gas emissions fell 0.3%, while coal emissions increased by 0.6%. The researchers present these findings at the U.N. climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkey.

cards.headline: Long-range drone strikes increase civilian suffering and infrastructure damage in Sudan

pages.text: The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) reports that unprecedented attacks on Sudan's infrastructure, including the use of drones traveling up to 1,500 kilometers, are increasing the suffering of non-combatants. The strikes target civilians, markets, and key public infrastructure, hindering aid efforts in a country where well over 15 million people urgently require shelter. This escalation occurs amid ongoing fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), former allies who became military rivals when the conflict began in mid-April 2023. UNICEF official Mr. Elder noted that while suicide drones were used several years ago, the last 12 months have seen the use of increasingly accurate long-range drones. In October, humanitarian agencies were unable to ascertain who was responsible for at least 15 strikes on Sudanese power stations.

In Sudan's southeastern Blue Nile State, Kurmuk Commissioner Abdel Ati Mohamed al-Faki attributed an attack to the RSF that killed nine displaced people and injured several others. The attack occurred as a group of displaced people traveled from the village of Bani Shako in Kurmuk locality toward Damazin, the capital of Blue Nile. Local officials stated that drone attacks on villages and residential gatherings in Kurmuk have increased in recent months, causing civilian casualties and displacement toward Damazin. Concurrently, a Sudanese military source reported that the SAF intensified air operations against positions held by the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North, in several areas of the region. In El Obeid, UN Human Rights Council investigators report that civilians live in constant fear of drone attacks.

cards.headline: Roshel Inc. to buy Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario

pages.text: Canadian armoured vehicle maker Roshel Inc. will acquire the idled Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario, for an undisclosed amount, according to an announcement from the companies. Roshel Inc. will also acquire associated equipment from the automaker. Stellantis stated the announcement is intended to create a path to return the Brampton Assembly Plant to productive industrial use. The two companies said they are exploring future collaboration regarding vehicle technologies and related services within the defence industry.

Unifor, the union representing Canadian workers at Stellantis, has criticized the sale. Unifor national president Lana Payne called the sale an “unacceptable outcome” and the “worst-case scenario” for the union and its members. Payne stated that closing and selling the plant cuts Canada's auto vehicle production capacity by 10 per cent. She added that the loss of capacity is often permanent and affects thousands of union jobs and thousands more along the supply chain. Payne also characterized the sale as an “underhanded deal” and a failure of national auto strategy.

cards.headline: University of Waterloo student pleads not guilty to false statements charge in U.S. court

pages.text: Weiheng (Billy) Zeng, a Chinese citizen studying at the University of Waterloo, has pleaded not guilty in a U.S. federal court following an FBI counter-intelligence investigation. Zeng was arraigned in U.S. District Court in Detroit on a single count of making false statements to U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents, according to public records reviewed by CBC News. A prosecutor described the case as involving “espionage-type activities.”

Court documents state that Zeng was questioned by U.S. federal agents on Aug. 23 while attempting to enter Michigan after crossing the Ambassador Bridge from Windsor, Ontario. Following three interviews, Zeng admitted to accepting paid “taskings” on behalf of someone he believed was linked to the Chinese government, according to a sworn affidavit filed in court by FBI special agent Robert Holbrook.

cards.headline: Payments Canada launches real-time rail national payment system

pages.text: Payments Canada has launched its real-time rail national payment system, a platform designed to allow participating members to exchange, clear, and settle payments securely in real time. The system is expected to speed day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by allowing near-instant payments clearing 24 hours a day. This launch follows a delay from an original target to have the system in place by 2019. Payments Canada CEO Susan Hawkins stated in a news release that the launch marks the beginning of a new era for payments in the country and provides a modern foundation for the payment ecosystem as a national asset designed specifically for Canada.

The real-time rail system is expected to generate savings through lower processing costs, reduced use of cheques and cash, and a shorter period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to recipients. Transactions that pass through Payments Canada systems include direct deposits, debit card payments, bill payments, wire payments, pre-authorized debits, and cheques. Henry Kim, a professor at York University's Schulich School of Business, said the announcement is a step in the right direction, noting that real-time settlement already exists in the U.S. and that the move helps Canada keep up with the rest of the world.

Initial participants in the new system include Bank of America, Digital Commerce Bank, DoBusiness.com, Koho, Paramount Commerce, Peoples Trust Co., Questbank, and Wealthsimple. Additional participants, including all major Canadian financial institutions, are expected to be added in the coming months.

cards.headline: 39 bodies recovered after migrant boat capsizes off the coast of Senegal

pages.text: The bodies of 39 people were recovered from beaches near Lompoul after an overcrowded pirogue, a traditional boat, capsized off the coast of Senegal on November 6, 2026. The disaster is one of the deadliest migrant boat tragedies in recent years, leaving families in northeastern Senegal mourning the loss of loved ones. Many of the deceased were young people who had embarked on the sea crossing from West Africa toward Europe in search of work and better opportunities to support their relatives at home.

The tragedy has left several households facing the sudden loss of family members who provided financial support. For many in Senegal, migration is a response to economic hardship intended to provide a better future for relatives. Beyond the immediate deaths, the disaster has raised fears among the families left behind regarding the future of others who may still be tempted to attempt the same perilous journey.

cards.headline: Trump says Iran war is 'effectively over' as Tehran denies planned talks

pages.text: U.S. President Donald Trump stated on November 9, 2026, that there is momentum toward ending the war with Iran, declaring that the country is “militarily, is effectively over.” While Trump told reporters at a White House press briefing that further strikes are “quite unlikely,” he maintained that the U.S. remains “locked and loaded” if it must return to military action. Following the statement, Brent crude futures fell to $92 a barrel as expectations grew regarding a potential end to the conflict. The U.S. has been conducting a massive naval blockade and the Iron Gate land operation, a CENTCOM task force designed to block the transfer of sanctioned goods, illicit revenues, and advanced weapons across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.

During his first meeting with a foreign leader since his party's midterm election losses, Trump met at the White House with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, a key mediator in the war. Trump reported on Truth Social that the leaders had an “excellent conversation” regarding the Islamic Republic of Iran, noting that Gulf states—including Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, and Kuwait—prefer the status quo over continued strikes. Al Thani, who also met with Vice President JD Vance in Washington, described the discussions as a way to advance negotiations and achieve regional peace. However, Iranian officials have disputed the possibility of imminent diplomatic breakthroughs. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi denied reports that Qatar would host a meeting between Vance and Mohsen Rezaei, the Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council. While Turkish intelligence service chief Ibrahim Kalin suggested such a meeting in Qatar could provide a breakthrough, Rezaei dismissed reports of talks as “fake news,” accusing the U.S. of acting like a “desperate gambler.”

Despite the rhetoric of a nearing end to the conflict, Iranian authorities reported that strikes are continuing on the ground. A provincial deputy governor stated on state television that the island of Qeshm, located in the Strait of Hormuz, was targeted overnight. Iranian officials have expressed continued defiance; Tehran's top negotiator Mahammad Bagher Ghalibaf claimed on X that the U.S. is being pushed deeper into conflict by Israel. Additionally, the Tasnim news agency, citing a senior Iranian security official, stated that Iran's negotiating position remains unchanged and that the country will not hold talks with the U.S. until Washington takes concrete steps regarding Iran's seven conditions. Trump emphasized that while momentum is positive, all parties agree that Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon, a point he stated is not open to negotiation.

cards.headline: Garment protests shut more than 100 factories in Ashulia, Bangladesh

pages.text: Apparel workers in the Ashulia industrial belt on the outskirts of Dhaka, Bangladesh, have staged protests that prompted the closure of more than 100 garment factories. The demonstrations included blockades on the Baipail-Abdullahpur road in Jamgora, which began around 10:30 am after workers from several units walked out of their workplaces to press for specific demands. These units included Envoy, Hollywood, The Rose, and Ha-Meem Group’s Next Collections. According to reports from bdnews24.com, witnesses stated that workers arrived at various factories across the industrial zone and clocked in as usual before the walkouts occurred. The protesters are demanding a Tk 30,000 minimum wage, an end to arbitrary “blacklisting,” the reinstatement of laid-off colleagues, and the release of arrested workers. Clashes and scuffles erupted between the workers and law-enforcing agencies, leading police to fire rubber bullets, tear gas canisters, and stun grenades to disperse the crowds.

cards.headline: Syria and Jordan sign 11 agreements to deepen economic cooperation

pages.text: Syria and Jordan have signed 11 agreements covering investment, agriculture, transport, and several other sectors to advance joint development projects and deepen economic cooperation. The agreements, which include eight memorandums of understanding, two executive programs, and one cooperation protocol, were signed in Damascus following the third session of the Syrian-Jordanian Higher Coordination Council held from Nov. 8 to 9. The council was co-chaired by Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan Al-Shaibani and Jordanian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, according to the Syria News Agency (SANA). These pacts come as both nations attempt to sustain a rapprochement that has been strained by deadly Jordanian airstrikes in October. The agreements aim to repair relations while a joint investigation addresses the fallout from that incident, which threatened to derail a broader reset in relations following the ouster of President Bashar al-Assad nearly two years ago, according to Al-Monitor.

The signed agreements cover a wide range of sectors, including food security, agriculture, the environment, water, railway transport, youth, public administration, civil aviation, higher education, scientific research, and education. To facilitate trade, the council emphasized addressing technical, logistical, and legislative challenges that affect trade flows and the development of joint supply chains, particularly in the food, pharmaceutical, and reconstruction-related industries, SANA reported. The two sides also discussed expanding activities within the Syrian-Jordanian Joint Free Zone and exploring the establishment of a joint economic city along their border to host industrial, production, and service activities to attract investment. Additionally, the council emphasized the need to activate the Joint Jordanian-Syrian Business Council and strengthen partnerships between private-sector institutions in both countries.

The economic agreements follow a significant increase in trade between the two nations. According to Amman Chamber of Commerce figures reported by the Jordan news agency, Petra, trade reached 334 million Jordanian dinars ($471 million) in 2025, nearly three times the 116 million dinars recorded in 2024. Of that 2025 total, Jordanian exports to Syria amounted to 252 million dinars, led by industrial and construction products such as iron, cement, marble, and specialized chemical products. Imports from Syria reached 82 million dinars, consisting mainly of raw materials and agricultural commodities. Discussions also addressed energy needs, specifically ways to meet Syria's natural gas requirements, including the possibility of supplying industrial facilities in southern Syria with compressed natural gas from Jordan’s Risha gas field. Furthermore, the council discussed mechanisms to develop and finance priority projects, including initiatives identified by Syria for potential financing through a dedicated Syrian Investment Fund for reconstruction, in coordination with financing institutions and donors.

cards.headline: Federal Express to pay $2.975 million fine for California privacy violations

pages.text: The California Privacy Protection Agency (CalPrivacy) Board has ordered shipping and logistics specialist Federal Express Corporation to pay a $2.975 million administrative fine and change its business practices to resolve claims that the company violated the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). The decision follows allegations that the company failed to respect privacy rights, including the implementation of functionality for opt-out preference signals. Acting Deputy Director of Enforcement Lara Kehoe Hoffman stated that the time for implementing such disclosures and functionality has long passed. In addition to the fine, the Board ordered Federal Express to comply with specific requirements for testing, monitoring, and risk-mitigation.

The ruling clarifies the scope of the CCPA, which is a law designed to protect the personal information of California residents. Executive Deputy Director Tom Kemp noted that the decision confirms the CCPA protects Californians from online surveillance even within a business-to-business (B2B) setting. Kemp stated that businesses must assess whether their B2B operations respect the privacy rights of individuals. The case was handled by Enforcement Division Attorneys Lisa B. Kim and Michael Meyer, with investigative assistance from Research Technologists Nikita Samarin and Primal Wijesekera.

cards.headline: Italy seeks parliamentary approval to increase F-35 fighter jet spending by €7.28 billion

pages.text: The Italian government is seeking parliamentary approval to increase planned investment in F-35 fighter jets by €7.28 billion ($8.17 billion), according to a parliamentary document. This increase would raise the program's overall cost by more than 50 percent, bringing total spending to €20.8 billion. The original program was approved in 2009 with a planned budget of €13.5 billion. The new investment is scheduled to begin and run through 2039.

The government stated the cost revision reflects technological upgrades, stricter security requirements, inflation, and changes in the euro-dollar exchange rate. This funding increase occurs as European countries increase defense spending following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and other security concerns. Italy has pledged to gradually raise military expenditure and accelerate investment in advanced military capabilities as allies call for stronger European defense.

cards.headline: Former Macau lawmaker sentenced to 12.5 years in prison under national security law

pages.text: On November 6, 2026, the Macau Court of First Instance sentenced 69-year-old former lawmaker Au Kam San to 12.5 years in prison, marking the first conviction under the Chinese territory's national security law. Au, who served in Macau’s legislature for more than 20 years and acted as a current affairs commentator following his 2021 retirement, was convicted of one count of subverting state power, three counts of contacting foreign organizations to endanger national security, and one count of violating confidentiality. The trial was conducted behind closed doors, leading international observers and rights groups to criticize the verdict as a “bogus prosecution” involving “serious violations of his right to a fair trial.”

cards.headline: Ontario lacks licensing system for private ownership of lions and tigers

pages.text: Provincial authorities in Ontario do not know how many lions or tigers are kept in private backyards across the province because Ontario is the only province in Canada without a licensing or permit system for keeping non-native wild animals. This lack of provincial oversight leaves it to individual municipalities to decide which species residents are permitted to own. In the rural municipality of Wainfleet, located 43 kilometres southwest of Niagara Falls, the township established its own rules in 2018 to provide local authorities with tools to address the presence of dangerous exotic animals.

Mark Tardif, the chief bylaw officer in Wainfleet, has managed encounters with a wide range of exotic animals, including primates, sugar gliders (a type of exotic gliding possum), pythons, tigers, a jaguar, lemurs, kangaroos, water buffaloes, and many snakes. Tardif noted his experience includes policing approximately five or six tigers, a jaguar, lemurs, kangaroos, and water buffaloes. His work has also involved responding to dozens of animal escapes from a roadside zoo called Ringtail Ranch. This spring, a Wainfleet resident named Zohaib Masood kept several tigers on a local property; a juvenile tiger and a hyena from that property were seized by an Ontario animal welfare services inspector. Masood was also documented with two adult tigers and a hyena. When responding to calls involving big cats, Tardif stated he leaves his vehicle running and the door open to provide an escape route, noting his protective vest was not designed for such encounters.

cards.headline: Canadian ultramarathoner Stephanie Case becomes first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica

pages.text: Canadian ultramarathoner Stephanie Case became the first woman to run 100 miles, or 160.9 kilometres, in Antarctica on November 8, 2026. Case, 44, completed the Antarctic Ice Ultra in Queen Maud Land, Eastern Antarctica, with a finishing time of 17:31:39. She carried a Canadian flag and stated that the achievement helps put women on the map in a location she referred to as the “womanless continent.”

The race took place on the southernmost continent, which is covered by the world's largest ice sheet. For safety reasons, the course consisted of a 4.2-kilometre looped circuit around a basecamp. To complete the 100-mile distance, runners completed the loop 38 times plus an additional 300 metres. Case said she managed the distance by focusing on 10 loops at a time to reach a full marathon distance before stopping to warm up in an aid tent.

Case told CBC News that while she had an idea of what to expect, she had never experienced such an extreme environment. She noted that the race, held on the coldest and windiest continent, caused her to rethink her life choices at times. Organizers describe the Antarctic Ice Ultra as an ultimate test of human endurance. Runners have participated in the event since its inaugural race in 2024.

cards.headline: Hydrocarbon discovery announced in offshore Ghana's Deepwater Cape Three Points block

pages.text: President John Dramani Mahama announced a new hydrocarbon discovery at the N1 GDA 9 1 X well in the Deepwater Cape Three Points contract area, located in the Tano Basin offshore Ghana. Speaking on November 10, 2026, at the 2026 Petroleum Commission Local Content Conference and Exhibition in the Western region, Mahama stated the discovery was made by Planet 1 Oil and Gas Limited in partnership with Bowler Upstream Limited and the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC). The find represents Ghana's first successful test of a Cenomanian-Turonian carbonate play as a primary exploration target, with the well also targeting the Albian formation as a secondary exploration objective.

The discovery adds to existing exploration activity in the Tano Basin, one of Ghana's offshore petroleum areas. Before any decisions regarding development are made, further appraisal work is required to determine the commercial potential and the extent of the discovery.

cards.headline: Bangladesh faces rising debt to finance climate transition through loans rather than grants

pages.text: Bangladesh is increasingly burdened by debt as it finances its clean-energy transition largely through loans instead of grants, according to a study by the Dhaka-based think tank Change Initiative (CI). A decade after the Paris Agreement pledged to support climate-vulnerable nations, researchers say the trend forces the country to borrow heavily to address a crisis it did little to create. M Zakir Hossain Khan, chief executive of Change Initiative, stated that the most climate-vulnerable countries are being forced to borrow their way through a crisis they did not cause, describing the situation as a second injury written into a contract. Between 2002 and 2023, Bangladesh received approximately $2.54 billion in identified energy-sector climate finance. Of that amount, 92 percent, or roughly $2.34 billion, came as loans, while grants accounted for only 8 percent, or around $203 million.

The financial pressure coincides with ambitious national energy and climate goals. A World Bank report published July 22 stated that renewable energy currently supplies only 1.5 percent of electricity in Bangladesh’s national grid. However, the country's Renewable Energy Policy 2025 aims to increase the renewable share to 20 percent by 2030 and 30 percent by 2040. To implement the third mitigation component of its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) submitted to the UN, Bangladesh will require $116.18 billion, with $90.23 billion of that amount contingent on international support.

In addition to energy transitions, Bangladesh must fund large-scale adaptation efforts. The National Adaptation Plan (2023-2050) identifies 113 major interventions across 11 climate-stressed regions, including the construction of sea dikes, cyclone shelters, and integrated management of coastal polders to protect against storm surges, sea-level rise, and extreme weather. Implementing these interventions is estimated to require more than $230 billion, with nearly three-quarters of that total needed by 2040.

cards.headline: Five killed as landslide hits displaced families' camp in Gaza

pages.text: A sand bank collapse triggered by high winds and heavy rain killed five people and crushed at least three tents south of Deir al-Balah in Gaza on November 8, 2026. The landslide occurred at a camp for displaced families, where witnesses described a frantic struggle to save those buried under sand and rocks. Among the dead were a mother and her two children, aged six and eight. The children's father survived because he was outside the family tent at the time; Abdul Karim al-Sahhar, 30, said one of the children had called him to come and eat with them just before the collapse. Al-Sahhar, who is originally from Izbat Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza, described the scene as a “horrifying sight,” noting that the family's tent had completely disappeared and the victims were not moving or making a sound.

cards.headline: Discovery of previously unaccounted for North Atlantic right whale calf near Quebec provides hope for species

pages.text: Scientists discovered a 6,804-kilogram North Atlantic right whale calf swimming with its mother off Anticosti Island, Quebec, in September. The calf had previously evaded researchers who track the endangered species' population. Amy Warren, a scientist at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center, told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal that she was initially skeptical of the find, but she and her colleagues confirmed the discovery by identifying the mother and comparing the calf's distinctive markings to existing records. This discovery brings the total number of baby right whales from the most recent birthing season to 24, which the aquarium stated is the fourth-highest count on record and the most productive year for the species since 2009.

The appearance of the calf offers a positive outlook for a species facing significant threats. According to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, there are only 380 North Atlantic right whales in the world. As of November 9, 2026, there are approximately 70 known reproductive-age females alive. The population fell by 25 per cent between 2010 and 2020. Warren noted that warming oceans are forcing the whales away from protected areas and into locations where they are vulnerable to entanglement in commercial fishing gear and collisions with large ships. Warren said that seeing so many calves is positive for scientists who frequently document the scars and injuries resulting from these traumatic events.

cards.headline: Saudi wilderness guide rescues elderly couple from floodwaters in Madinah region

pages.text: Tariq Marghalani, a Saudi adventurer and certified hiking and cave tourism guide, rescued an elderly man and his wife after their four-wheel-drive vehicle became trapped in fast-moving floodwaters west of Madinah on the morning of November 7, 2026. The flash floods were triggered by rainfall that affected several parts of the Madinah region. Marghalani, who also serves as a wilderness medic, was traveling through Badr Governorate with members of the Taiba Hiking Team for a paragliding outing when the group spotted the vehicle surrounded by rushing water.

Upon seeing the scene, Marghalani used climbing gear, including ropes and harnesses, to reach the vehicle. He reported to Arab News that he did not know how many people were inside and that his only objective was to rescue whoever was trapped. The elderly couple had taken refuge in the rear of the vehicle but were unable to open the back door due to the force of the water. Marghalani assessed whether to extract the occupants through a narrow side window or attempt to force open a submerged door. During the rescue, the elderly husband insisted that his wife be evacuated first.

cards.headline: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah border crossing and Gaza aid facilities

pages.text: Seven-time Formula 1 world champion Lewis Hamilton visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip and toured logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent. The visit, which included meeting with organizations sending humanitarian aid to the territory, followed Hamilton's 400th race start at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on November 8, 2026. Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai where Rafah is located, stated the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza. During the tour of the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with the Arabic greeting “Assalamu alaikum” and spoke briefly with officials and workers.

Hamilton has frequently called for peace and a ceasefire, using social media to post about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza. He stated, “I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage.” While a ceasefire agreement has halted major combat operations in Gaza, an independent commission of UN experts reported that the amount of aid entering the strip remains far below the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day. The commission also noted that Israeli forces have expanded their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, and that airstrikes and fire along the advancing front have killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys, and 11 girls.

cards.headline: Ghanaian man sentenced to two years in prison for using fraudulent Canadian passport 16 times

pages.text: Jefferson Zormelo, a 22-year-old Ghanaian, was sentenced to two years in prison in Calgary, Alberta, on Monday, November 9, 2026, for violating the Canadian Citizenship Act. Zormelo pleaded guilty to using a fraudulent Canadian passport to enter and leave Canada 16 times through international airports in Montreal, Toronto, and Halifax. Justice Karen Molle stated the offense undermined the integrity of Canada's citizenship system and warned that such fraudulent use could threaten national security, public safety, and the country's international reputation. After receiving credit for time already served since his arrest, Zormelo has approximately 14 months remaining to serve.

Zormelo arrived in Canada in 2021 on a study permit, but immigration authorities determined in 2024 that he was no longer enrolled in school and issued an exclusion order for his removal from the country. According to an agreed statement of facts filed in court, Zormelo subsequently obtained identification documents, including proof of Canadian citizenship, under a false identity. He secured a Canadian passport in December 2024 issued in the name of Mitchell Leblanc. He used this passport to travel 16 times over the following 15 months.

The activity ended in April 2026 when Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officers arrested Zormelo in Calgary. The arrest occurred after he presented a fraudulent permanent resident card bearing the Leblanc identity to officials at the United States Consulate. A search of his hotel room uncovered the fraudulent Canadian passport and other items. During sentencing, prosecutor Tyler Lord sought a five-year prison term, while defense lawyer Devin Frank requested a sentence equivalent to the time Zormelo had already spent in custody.

cards.headline: Budget restraints limit paid Remembrance Day participation for 31 Canadian Brigade

pages.text: A military reserve unit in southwestern Ontario has capped the number of soldiers it will pay to attend Remembrance Day services due to internal budget restraints. Leaked internal emails involving members of 31 Canadian Brigade show that local commanders have been forced to limit paid attendance to 50 troops per unit. This decision means 650 soldiers out of a total strength of 2,400 can participate in local ceremonies. Reservists normally receive a half-day's pay for these ceremonial events, according to one of the internal emails. The brigade is headquartered at Wolseley Barracks in London, Ontario, and includes 13 units located across the region, including St. Thomas, Waterloo, and Hamilton.

In an Oct. 9 internal email, 31 Canadian Brigade commander Col. Blair Ashford wrote that he decided to increase the allotment to 50 soldiers per unit, calling it a “defensible number” because it matches the number of soldiers that turn out for exercises. Ashford alluded to having to make a final choice between ceremonies and the one day a week of training units are expected to complete. While the initial plan reportedly involved funding fewer than 50 soldiers per unit, the current cap has not been well received by troops, many of whom told CBC News that maximum participation was encouraged in the past.

cards.headline: Saudi Arabia manufacturing registrations rise 18 percent

pages.text: Saudi Arabia’s manufacturing sector reached 255,188 business registrations by the end of the third quarter of 2026, an 18 percent annual increase from 215,697 during the same period of 2025, according to the Ministry of Commerce. These figures represent active commercial registrations for specific business activities but do not indicate the number of factories that began production or the total volume of industrial output. The growth occurs as the Kingdom seeks to expand its industrial and mining base, develop domestic supply chains, and increase manufacturing capabilities in sectors related to the automotive industry and the energy transition. This expansion aligns with Saudi Vision 2030, a framework aimed at diversifying the economic base and stimulating the growth of small and medium-sized enterprises. The Ministry of Commerce attributed the increases to efforts to support industry and improve the use of natural resources, noting that the growth reflects expanding commercial and investment opportunities. The Kingdom is working toward a target of 36,000 factories by 2035, with a goal for the industrial sector's contribution to gross domestic product to reach SR1.4 trillion ($372.2 billion), according to targets outlined by the deputy minister of industry and mineral resources for industrial affairs at the Budget Forum 2026.

Specific industrial subsectors saw significant registration growth during the period ending in September. Registrations for the manufacture and assembly of automobile engines and their components increased 45 percent to 1,207, up from 832 a year earlier. Registrations for the manufacture of solar panels and their components rose 33 percent to 1,700, compared to 1,270 during the corresponding period of 2025. Additionally, the Saudi Press Agency reported that registrations in mining and quarrying grew 13 percent to 12,831 from 11,263. These developments reflect broader growth in the Saudi Arabian business sector; a separate Ministry of Commerce bulletin published in July stated that the country issued more than 71,000 new commercial registrations in the second quarter of 2026, bringing the total number of existing registrations across the country to more than 1.91 million.

cards.headline: Saudi Energy nine-month profit rises 4.3% to $3.2 billion

pages.text: Saudi Energy reported a 4.3 percent year-on-year increase in net profit to SR12.1 billion ($3.2 billion) during the first nine months of 2026. The company attributed the growth to an expanding regulated asset base—the value of assets used to determine permitted revenue—and higher revenue from projects. During the same period, revenue rose 11.5 percent to SR87.2 billion, driven by increased income from project development and management contracts, customer growth, and higher regulated revenue, including pass-through costs. The company's regulated asset base reached SR278.8 billion at the end of September, a 16.6 percent year-on-year increase, as completed transmission and distribution projects entered service.

In the third quarter, Saudi Energy's net profit increased 0.4 percent to SR5.4 billion, while revenue grew 12.9 percent to SR35 billion. These quarterly results were supported by higher gross profit, increased earnings from equity-accounted investments, and lower expected credit-loss provisions, though gains were partly offset by increased net financing costs, higher administrative expenses, and lower other income. For the full nine-month period, operating profit rose 4.7 percent to SR16.9 billion, and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization increased 6.6 percent to SR34.7 billion. Adjusted capital expenditure, which excluded accruals and customer-funded transmission and distribution projects, stood at SR59.6 billion, with spending directed toward distribution, generation, battery storage, and transmission expansion.

The financial results occur as Saudi Arabia works to reshape its electricity sector, aiming for a 2030 generation mix of approximately 50 percent natural gas and 50 percent renewable energy while phasing out liquid fuels for power generation. CEO Khalid Al-Ghamdi stated that the company achieved its 2026 target by energizing 22 GWh (gigawatt-hour) of battery storage to support greater renewable integration and a more flexible grid. By the end of September, grid-connected renewable capacity reached approximately 19.3 GW. Additionally, the company reported that the peak electricity load in the Kingdom reached 79,045 megawatts, which is 2.5 percent above the 2025 peak.

cards.headline: Bangladesh ready-made garment exports to non-traditional markets rise 9.30 percent

pages.text: Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) exports to non-traditional markets grew 9.30 percent to US$2.37 billion during the July-October period of FY2026-27, according to Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data compiled by Bangladesh Apparel Voice (BAV). This period saw an increase from $2.17 billion in the same period a year earlier. The growth was largely driven by a sharp increase in exports to Turkey, which more than doubled during the period. Exports to Turkey surged 107.05 percent to $206.5 million from $99.7 million, adding $106.8 million to the overall export growth of $201.8 million across non-traditional markets. Turkey alone contributed around 53 percent of the total increase, and its share of Bangladesh’s RMG exports to non-traditional markets nearly doubled from 4.60 percent to 8.71 percent. Without the performance in Turkey, export growth across these markets would have been limited to around 4.6 percent.

Among the major non-traditional destinations, Japan remained the largest market, with exports reaching $437.3 million, up 2.40 percent from the corresponding period a year earlier. Japan accounted for 18.44 percent of total exports to non-traditional markets. Exports to Australia increased 3.01 percent to $264 million, while shipments to South Korea grew 5.82 percent to $151.3 million. Conversely, exports to India declined 5.38 percent to $250.9 million. Exports to markets outside the top five destinations rose 8.48 percent to $1.06 billion, accounting for 44.76 percent of Bangladesh’s total RMG exports to non-traditional markets. In October alone, Bangladesh’s RMG exports to non-traditional markets increased 8.99 percent to $559.7 million.

cards.headline: Brazil deploys National Public Security Force to Ituna/Itatá Indigenous Territory following invasion

pages.text: Brazil has deployed the National Public Security Force to the Ituna/Itatá Indigenous Territory in Pará, northern Brazil, to support the country’s Indigenous Affairs Agency (Funai) in protecting the land. A spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice and Public Security (MJSP) told Mongabay that the deployment is underway and troops are already in the region. The deployment is scheduled for a period of 180 days following an invasion approximately two months ago by more than 500 people into the territory, where the isolated Igarapé Ipiaçava Indigenous people live. This security response follows an Aug. 26 order from a federal court requiring the government to deploy a security team within 48 hours to respond to the invasion.

The invasion occurred in the weeks after the approval of a new state law in Pará in August 2026, which created the Bacajaí Environmental Protection Area (APA Bacajaí). This law allows private landowners to build homes and raise livestock in the area. However, the federal government maintains the state law is invalid because the APA Bacajaí completely overlaps with the federally protected Indigenous land. During the invasion, hundreds of people smashed through security gates, tore down warning signs, and established camps inside the territory. A Mongabay investigation published in October found that a coordinated social media campaign involving politicians and influential agribusiness figures helped push the invasion, and that the fast-tracked law helped legitimize and encourage the influx of people.

Environmental indicators within the territory have changed since the law's passage and the subsequent invasion. Forest fire alerts inside Ituna/Itatá rose from zero alerts in August to 23 signs of fires by October.

cards.headline: Sales of bottled water and tinned food rise following 'Be Ready' campaign launch

pages.text: Sales of bottled water, hand sanitiser, and tinned or jarred goods increased in the 10 days following the launch of the government's “Be Ready” emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, according to research from retail firm Worldpanel by Numerator. The campaign encouraged households to stock up on essentials, such as three days' worth of food and water, to prepare for potential disruptions to essential services caused by cyberattacks or severe weather. Other recommended items included cash, a torch, and wet wipes. While the surge in sales indicates people responded to the campaign, Worldpanel stated that households were stockpiling essentials rather than panic buying. Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator, noted that less than a third of households bought bottled water in October and that growth resulted from more people adding recommended checklist items to their weekly shops rather than shoppers piling trolleys high.

Data from Worldpanel by Numerator shows hand sanitiser sales rose 83%, bottled water sales rose 67%, and sales of tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%. Specifically, sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from £58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to £79.5m over the same period in 2026. Bottled water sales increased from £13.6m to £22.8m compared with the previous year, and hand sanitiser sales rose from £497,000 to £908,000. Worldpanel reported that the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat after the campaign launch, though the typical amount purchased remained at 500g. Food firm Princes also reported that demand for tinned vegetables, meat, and tuna had risen following the government campaign.

cards.headline: Paleontologists identify 450-million-year-old fossil preserving rare soft tissue

pages.text: Paleontologists at the University of Oklahoma have identified an exceptionally rare fossil of an extinct crinoid species, Dendrocrinus simcoensis, that preserves delicate soft tissue structures. The specimen dates back more than 450 million years, a period long before dinosaurs appeared and before plants and animals were widespread on land. While scientists have discovered millions of crinoid fossils, nearly all preserve only hard skeletal structures; this discovery provides a rare opportunity to study how early marine animals lived, fed, and evolved by examining parts that typically decay before fossilization can occur.

Crinoids are marine animals related to modern starfish that often resemble underwater flowers with branching arms extending from a central body. More than 450 million years ago, these creatures thrived in Earth's earliest coral reefs. Because soft tissues like skin, eyes, or internal organs are usually the first parts to decay after an animal dies, most fossils consist only of hard parts such as bones, teeth, or shells. Dr. Lena Cole, a University of Oklahoma paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, noted that soft tissue preservation requires incredibly rare environmental conditions that act like a natural refrigerator or vacuum-sealer.

cards.headline: Alzheimer's genetic mutations may interfere with nerves controlling muscle movement outside the brain

pages.text: Genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's disease can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord, according to research from the University of Central Florida (UCF). The study suggests that physical symptoms, such as changes in balance, coordination, or gait, may develop outside the central nervous system and could serve as early warning signs of the disease before memory loss or cognitive decline becomes apparent. This discovery addresses whether movement problems in patients are merely consequences of brain damage or if the disease interferes directly with nerves elsewhere in the body. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

The research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang “Nadine” Guo, in collaboration with scientists from the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the team used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. Research Professor Guo stated that motor deficits may be an earlier indication of the disease and noted that detecting and intervening in these changes could potentially help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms.

cards.headline: Natural molecule may aid brain recovery after hemorrhagic stroke

pages.text: Research led by University of Manchester scientists suggests a naturally occurring molecule could lead to new treatments for intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH), a deadly form of stroke. ICH occurs when a blood vessel bursts and bleeds directly into the brain, leaking substances like iron that cause serious damage. Effective treatments for this condition currently remain limited. The study, published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation, identified a biological process in humans and mice that appears to help the brain manage the aftermath of bleeding to improve recovery. This clean-up process is critical because the breakdown of red blood cells can contribute to further brain damage following the initial stroke.

The Medical Research Council funded study focused on an enzyme called cholesterol 25-hydroxylase (CH25H), which converts cholesterol into a molecule called 25-hydroxycholesterol (25HC). Researchers found increased levels of CH25H in brain tissue from people who had suffered ICH, specifically within the immune cells surrounding the site of the bleed. The enzyme appears to assist microglia—the brain's resident immune cells—in engulfing and removing red blood cells released into brain tissue after a haemorrhage. The process also influenced genes within the microglia responsible for processing fats and cholesterol and clearing cellular debris.

In experiments involving mice, those genetically lacking Ch25h experienced worse neurological symptoms, greater tissue damage, and increased iron accumulation following an experimentally induced brain haemorrhage. When Ch25h was absent, the immune cells were less effective at engulfing red blood cells and accumulated more fatty droplets inside them. Conversely, treating mice with 25HC improved functional recovery and reduced signs of brain damage. Researchers suggest this natural process could potentially be harnessed to improve recovery for patients by limiting the harmful effects of bleeding.

cards.headline: Short-eared owls identified as cause of 1,700-year-old frog bone discovery

pages.text: Scientists have identified short-eared owls and hen harriers as the cause of a massive ancient frog cemetery near Cambridge. Researchers from Bournemouth University and the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) determined that these birds of prey were responsible for the remains found in a single ditch near an Iron Age roundhouse at Bar Hill. Between 2016 and 2018, approximately 8,000 ancient frog bones were discovered at the site. Radiocarbon dating conducted by the University of Vienna showed the remains date back 1,700 years to the Roman period. The researchers reached this conclusion by comparing damage to the frog bones with previous studies, concluding the bones were left behind after the birds ate the frogs.

A new method of analysis used by the Bournemouth University team revealed that most of the frogs died young, having been eaten during the winter of their first year of life. Archaeological evidence indicated that the ditch filled within a single year. During the Roman period, the fen wetlands in the valley were retreating, which created conditions ideal for the frogs to breed. However, large areas of woodland were gradually felled to provide grazing for livestock. This reduction in trees left the amphibians with less protection from grassland hunters. Dr. Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth University stated that the bones provide insights into the natural world and what wild animals were doing in the past, noting that archaeological sites do not often provide an 'owl's eye view' of history.

cards.headline: Neighboring planet's gravity tilts the orbit of the first known disappearing planet

pages.text: UCLA-led astronomers have discovered the first known “disappearing planet,” TOI-2535 b, located approximately 1,000 light-years away. While the planet appeared to vanish after researchers observed it transiting its star multiple times over seven years, the planet has not actually disappeared. Instead, gravity from a neighboring planet is tilting TOI-2535 b's orbit, changing its alignment relative to Earth. This shift means the planet no longer passes directly between its star and our line of sight, preventing the detection of its transits.

TOI-2535 b is a “hot Jupiter,” a type of gas giant that orbits extremely close to its host star. The planet completes an orbit in only 8.25 days, which is 10 times faster than the 88 days Mercury takes to orbit the Sun. The planet was originally identified using images from NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) of the TOI-2535 star system taken between April 2019 and March 2026. TESS detects planets by measuring transits, which are small changes in a star’s brightness that occur when a planet passes in front of the star and blocks some of its light. For a transit to be visible, there must be a precise alignment between the star, the planet, and the observer's line of sight.

cards.headline: Observing rodent cage matches can rewire mouse brains for fighting, study finds

pages.text: Brain scientists have found that mice can be primed for battle simply by watching other mice fight. In a study conducted at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, researchers observed that observing fighting matches can rewire a mouse's brain to resemble the brains of mice that actually participated in the fights. Annegret Falkner, an associate professor at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, explained that the researchers set up a platform above a cage to create a gladiator-style arena, allowing one mouse to watch two others swipe at each other below. While mice naturally fight in the wild to defend territories and form hierarchies, these laboratory matches functioned as a form of rodent wrestling performance.
